sourceTopic: Making Ten as an Addition Strategy

history.title: Find the Ten

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Making a ten can help you add. Use counters, pictures or fingers if they work for you. Take the time you need.

1. Read **Ten Is a Friendly Number** with a grown-up or a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Number Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Look at the **Ways to Make Ten** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **Makes Ten or Not?**
5. Try **Make-Ten Problems** with counters.
6. Take **Number Check** — say, point to or show each answer first.
7. Lock it in with **Remember the Partners**.
8. Read **Number Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Investigation: The Ten Frame Hunt**.

Your job this week: find ten of something at home and show two ways to split it. 🔟

Picture panels: Find and split ten; Fill the empty spaces; Make a ten first; Another way to make ten. Pictures have no printed labels. Count each object once. Captions explain how to read before-and-after pictures. Use counters, drawings, spoken answers or supported pointing. Educator review is pending.

history.title: Ten Is a Friendly Number
history.data:
## Ten Is a Friendly Number

Look at a ten frame. It has two rows of five spaces. Fill each space with one counter. Now you have **ten**!

Each whole number from zero to ten has a **partner** that makes ten. Six and four are partners. Seven and three are partners. Five and five are partners too. Ten and zero make ten: one group can be empty.

A number **bond** shows a whole and its parts. Here, our whole is ten.

Try 8 + 5 with counters. Eight needs two more to be ten. **Break** the five into two and three. Move the two to the eight. Now you have ten and three **left**. Ten and three make thirteen.

You moved counters between groups. You did not add any new counters or take any away. The **sum** stays the same.

Try 9 + 6. Nine needs one more. Break six into one and five. Move one to the nine. Ten and five make fifteen.

You can also count on or use a **double**, like 6 + 6. Different ways can help. Use counters, drawings or fingers if they work for you. Take the time you need.

Can you show one way to make ten?

history.title: Make-Ten Problems

steps.explanation: Look at the 8. It needs 2 more to make ten.
Break the 5 into 2 and 3. Give the 2 to the 8.
Now you have 10 and 3 left. 10 and 3 is 13.
Look at the 9. It needs 1 more to make ten.
Break the 6 into 1 and 5. Give the 1 to the 9.
Now you have 10 and 5 left. That is 15.
Look at the 7. It needs 3 more to make ten.
Break the 5 into 3 and 2. Give the 3 to the 7.
Now you have 10 and 2 left. That is 12.
Put six counters into a ten frame.
Count the empty spaces. There are four.
Fill those four spaces. Six and four make ten.
This one is a double. You may already know it.
If not, use the trick. The 6 needs 4 more to make ten.
Break the other 6 into 4 and 2. That gives 10 and 2, which is 12.

history.meta: 5 problems • use counters • steps read aloud

questions.question: Which two numbers are partners that make ten?
For 8 + 5, how much does the 8 need to make ten?
You break 5 into 2 and 3, and give the 2 away. What is left?
When you move some over to make a ten, what happens to the answer?
Show how to work out 7 + 6 by making a ten.
questions.expectedAnswer: The 7 needs 3 more to make ten. Break the 6 into 3 and 3. Give one 3 to the 7 to make ten. That leaves 3. Ten and 3 is 13.

questions.question: Your friend says 8 and 3 make ten. What would you tell them?
questions.expectedAnswer: They do not make ten. 8 and 3 make 11. The partner of 8 is 2, because 8 and 2 make ten.

reflections.text: Which partner is easiest for you to remember?
Was the trick fun or tricky? Tell why.

history.title: Number Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Why does a ten frame help?
data.answer: Two rows of five make ten. The spaces help you see how many you have and how many more you need.

data.question: Can I just count on my fingers?
data.answer: Yes. You can use fingers, counters, drawings or a ten frame. Choose a tool that works for you. Counting helps you explain your thinking.

data.question: Does the trick work for big numbers too? 🔢
data.answer: It does. Later you will make a hundred the same way. The same idea grows with you.

data.question: What if I forget a partner?
data.answer: Fill a ten frame with the number you have. Count the empty spaces. That tells how many more will make ten.

data.question: Is there more than one way to add? 🤔
data.answer: Lots of ways. You can count on. You can use a double. You can make a ten. They all give the same answer.

data.question: Do I have to use the trick every time?
data.answer: No. You can count on, use doubles or make a ten. Choose a way that helps you, and show how it works.

data.title: The Ten Frame Hunt
data.instructions: Find ten small things. Split them into two piles. Do it again a different way. Show what you found.
data.fitReason: Splitting a real ten many ways is how a first grader meets every number bond at once. Doing it with objects they chose makes the partners theirs instead of a list to memorise.

brief.context: Use ten teacher-provided counters, blocks or picture tokens and a ten frame. Move them, point while a partner moves them, or use a digital version.
brief.audience: The class, who will build one big wall of all the ways to make ten
brief.drivingQuestion: How many different ways can you split ten things into two piles?
brief.seedDirection: Start with all ten in one pile. Move one across at a time. Do not skip.
lockedLessonFacts: A ten frame has two rows of five spaces.
Each whole number from zero to ten has a partner that makes ten.
Six and four are partners. Seven and three are partners.
Moving some across does not change how many there are.
openQuestions: What do you notice when you move one across each time?
Do 6 and 4 and 4 and 6 give the same total? What changes about the groups?
How do you know when you have found them all?
stakeholders: Your partner who checks your counting
The teacher who puts the wall up
criteria: You always have ten things in total
Each way is drawn or shown with the two piles
You find at least four different ways
You say one thing you noticed
constraints: Ten things, no more and no fewer
Two groups each time; one group may be empty
Count, point, draw or explain with a partner
brief.deliverable: A page with your ways to make ten, each one drawn as two piles, and one sentence about something you noticed.

parallelExample.context: A student used ten buttons and kept losing count.
parallelExample.move: She put all ten in a line first. Then she moved one button across at a time and drew each step. She found every way and never lost count.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Moving one at a time meant she never had to start over, and the line kept all ten in sight.

supports.frameStarter: I have ____ in this pile and ____ in that pile. Together that is ____.
coachPrompts: What changed when you moved one across?
Have you found a way you have not drawn yet?

data.coachHint: Keep ten in total. Move one at a time. If left and right count as different, there are eleven pairs from 0 and 10 through 10 and 0. Ignoring order gives six pairs. One group can be empty.
data.sourceExcerpt: Each whole number from zero to ten has a partner that makes ten. Moving counters between groups keeps the total the same.
